title: Control Is Slipping Away Date Published: June 4, 2026 Original URL: https://radicalconformity.substack.com
author: Colin Gautrey
summary: Gautrey argues that most people do not lose agency through a single dramatic surrender but through the accumulation of small, apparently reasonable accommodations — deferred decisions, accepted directions without examination, paths of least resistance taken under pressure — until they wake to a life that is recognizably theirs but not deliberately chosen. The article names low-grade, persistent powerlessness — not the acute powerlessness of crisis, but the ongoing sense of being carried along by events — as the result of years of unchosen choices, and distinguishes it carefully from genuine external constraint. External forces (economic pressure, institutional demands, decision fatigue from the pace of change) accelerate the slippage, narrowing options in ways that begin to feel permanent and replacing active choice with the path of least resistance as the default. Social pressure compounds the effect: family, community, and professional expectations shape behavior in ways rarely examined, so that what feels like a personal decision is often a structural response to what the situation appears to require. Gautrey's central philosophical point is that the absence of deliberate choice is not the absence of choice: deferring a decision is a decision, accepting a direction without examining it is a decision, going along with what the situation seems to demand is a decision — and all of these are still creating a future. The article points toward his 'Radical Conformity' principles around decision-as-reality-creation and designing your future, suggesting that recovery from drifted agency is available but requires first recognizing the drift as a product of one's own unchosen choices rather than purely external forces.
points: Gautrey's insight that powerlessness often grows from inside rather than being imposed from outside reframes the recovery question: if the drift was produced by accumulated unchosen choices, it can be reversed by beginning to make deliberate ones — not by changing external circumstances first.

The 'series of small accommodations' framing is psychologically precise: each individual accommodation feels reasonable and even virtuous (deference, flexibility, not making waves), which is why the pattern is invisible until it has been running for years and the cumulative effect is felt.

Decision fatigue as an institutional force is underappreciated: the pace of modern organizational life generates so many micro-decisions that defaulting to the path of least resistance is a predictable and rational response — but it is also, as Gautrey argues, a mechanism through which agency is gradually transferred.

The distinction between 'being carried along by events' (a drift state) and 'choosing to adapt to circumstances' (a deliberate state) is not primarily about outcomes but about whether the person knows they are choosing, which requires regular deliberate reflection rather than just reacting to the immediate.

Social expectations are particularly insidious because they dress external constraint as internal preference: what feels like 'what I want' is often 'what the people around me expect,' and the two are only distinguishable through the kind of deliberate self-examination that drift specifically prevents.
quotes: Nobody wakes up and decides to hand control of their life to someone else. It happens differently. A series of small accommodations. Decisions deferred because the moment did not feel right. Directions accepted because the alternative required more than felt available.
Structures and systems absorbed into daily life until they feel like the natural order rather than choices that were ever made.

'Somehow it just feels like I'm being carried along by events, adrift.' 'I can't remember the last time I felt like I actually chose this.' These are not the words of people who have failed. They are the words of people who have been quietly losing ground for longer than they realised.

Economic pressure narrows options in ways that begin to feel permanent. Institutions make demands that feel non-negotiable. The pace of change produces a kind of decision fatigue where the path of least resistance becomes the default, not because it was chosen but because everything else required energy that was already stretched.

What makes this difficult to see is that the absence of deliberate choice is not the same as the absence of choice. Deferring a decision is a decision. Accepting a direction without examining it is a decision. Going along with what the situation seems to demand is a decision. These are still choices. They are still creating a future.
Powerlessness is not always imposed from outside. Much of the time it grows in the space left by decisions that were never made.
